newsitem.title: FRANCE: French women nearly double seats in parliament.
newsitem.headline: French women nearly double seats in parliament.

text.p: French women nearly doubled their tiny share of seats in parliament in Sunday's Socialist-led election victory, a muted feminine breakthrough in a nation once led by 15th century warrior Joan of Arc.

Final results on Monday showed that women won 62 seats, or 10.7 percent of the 577-member National Assembly, helped by a Socialist and Communist policy of fielding women candidates in 30 percent of all districts.
Women had just 32 seats, or 5.5 percent of the total, in the outgoing parliament, the lowest in the European Union.
Yet France is so far adrift from most of its EU partners that the surge was enough only to lift it past Greece into 14th place in the 15-nation group. Sweden tops the list with more than 40 percent.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, named prime minister on Monday, has said that a left-wing government would seek to boost women's role in government, including more cabinet posts.
"If there is a government of change, then it will be a government in which women will have major posts," Jospin told a news conference last month.
Among prominent Socialist women are Martine Aubry, tipped as employment minister, Elisabeth Guigou, a possible social affairs minister and Catherine Trautmann, favoured to take over urban affairs.
France has had one female prime minister, Socialist Edith Cresson, who lasted a scant 10 months before resigning in 1992 with her popularity at a record low.

She was the highest ranking woman since Joan of Arc led French armies against the English in the 15th century. Burned at the stake as a witch in 1431 after being betrayed to the English, Joan was canonized in 1921.
French women also trail in business -- the heads of France's 200 biggest French firms are, without exception, men.

Yet, in contrast to their lack of power overall, some French women have become icons -- from Nobel prize-winning scientist Marie Curie, who discovered radium, to Brigitte Bardot, who switched from actress and sex symbol to animal rights campaigner.
About 60 percent of women work, roughly the EU average. French women have overthrown Roman Catholic resistance to win liberal laws on issues ranging from child benefits to birth control and abortion.

Defeated conservative prime minister Alain Juppe, who resigned on Monday morning, came to office in May 1995 -- after the election of conservative President Jacques Chirac -- trumpeting a record 12 women in his cabinet, or 30 percent of ministers.

He sacked eight of them in a reshuffle later that year, cutting women's percentage in the cabinet to an unexceptional 13 percent and drawing charges that the so-called "Juppettes" were a gimmick to help secure Chirac's election.
Women only got the vote in France after the Liberation from the Nazis in 1944, decades after many other European nations.
And the 19th century Napoleonic legal code gave men sweeping powers over their wives that lasted well into the 20th century.
Napoleon once said a woman was "the property of man as a fruit tree belongs to a gardener".
